kangaroo-at-2019-junior-02.title: Minutes and seconds separately
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-02.body:
Six circuits take $6$ minutes and $6\cdot 11 = 66$ seconds. Since $66$ s $= 1$ min $6$ s, that is $7$ minutes $6$ seconds.

**Answer: (B) 7 minutes 6 seconds**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-02.title: Convert to seconds
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-02.body:
One circuit is $71$ s, six circuits $426$ s $= 7\cdot 60 + 6$ s $= 7$ min $6$ s.

**Answer: (B) 7 minutes 6 seconds**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-03.title: Mirror every letter and the order
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-03.body:
A mirror reverses left and right. So the board must show the mirror image of SHAVE: the letters in reverse order E, V, A, H, S, **and** each letter itself reflected. H, A and V are symmetric, but E and S must appear reversed. Only (E) has the reversed order with both a reversed E and a reversed S. (C) has a normal S and (D) a normal E, which would look reversed in the mirror.

**Answer: (E)**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-04.title: Smallest to largest
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-04.body:
The smallest sum is $1+1+1 = 3$ and the largest $6+6+6 = 18$. Every sum in between is possible: starting from $1,1,1$ you can raise one die by 1 at a time until all show 6. So the sums $3, 4, \ldots, 18$ occur: $18 - 3 + 1 = 16$ different sums.

**Answer: (C) 16**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-05.title: Read the scale on both sides
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-05.body:
For a tilted jug, the water forms a trapezoid in the side view. Its area (and so the amount of water) is the width of the jug times the *average* of the water heights measured along the two sides. Read off the water level on the scale marks on both sides of each tilted jug and take the average; compare it with the level in the upright jug (A).

For (C), (D) and (E) the averages equal the level of (A) — in each, what is missing on one side is gained on the other. Only in (B) does the average of the two side readings differ from the level in (A), so (B) is the jug with a different amount.

**Answer: (B)**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-06.title: Multiply
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-06.body:
She has 5 choices for the entrance and then 4 choices for a different exit: $5\cdot 4 = 20$ ways.

**Answer: (B) 20**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-06.title: Unordered pairs twice
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-06.body:
There are $\binom52 = 10$ pairs of gates, and each pair can be used in two directions (in through one, out through the other): $2\cdot 10 = 20$.

**Answer: (B) 20**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-07.title: Make them as equal as possible
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-07.body:
If the lightest weighs $a$, the others weigh at least $a+1$ and $a+2$, so $3a + 3 \le 97$, i.e. $a \le 31\frac13$, so $a \le 31$. And $31 + 32 + 34 = 97$ works. The answer is 31 kg.

**Answer: (C) 31**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-07.title: Check 32
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-07.body:
If the lightest weighed 32, the total would be at least $32 + 33 + 34 = 99 > 97$. So 32 is too much, and 31 works with $31, 32, 34$.

**Answer: (C) 31**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-08.title: Use the symmetry of the grid
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-08.body:
Both lines start at the bottom-left corner. The lower one goes 3 right and 2 up, the upper one 2 right and 3 up. These two lines are mirror images of each other in the diagonal of the square. So the lower line makes angle $\alpha$ with the bottom side, and the upper line makes the same angle $\alpha$ with the left side. The right angle at the corner is split into $\alpha + \beta + \alpha$, so $2\alpha + \beta = 90^\circ$.

**Answer: (B) $2\alpha + \beta = 90^\circ$**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-08.title: Rule out the others
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-08.body:
With $\tan\alpha = \frac23$ we get $\alpha \approx 33.7^\circ$ and then $\beta = 90^\circ - 2\alpha \approx 22.6^\circ$. So $\alpha\ne\beta$, $\alpha+\beta \approx 56.3^\circ$ (neither 60° nor 45°) and $2\beta + \alpha \approx 78.9^\circ$. Only (B) holds.

**Answer: (B) $2\alpha + \beta = 90^\circ$**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-09.title: Triangles between opposite sides
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-09.body:
A triangle whose base lies on one side of the square and whose apex lies on the opposite side has area $\frac12\cdot \text{base}\cdot 1$ — exactly half of the strip above its base.

In (B), (C), (D) and (E) the square is cut into such triangles that alternate black and white across the whole width, so in each case exactly half the square is black (in (E) the diagonal halves the square).

In (A) the triangles only cover part of the width, and in addition there is a full-height black bar: the triangles give half of their strips, and the bar is completely black. So in (A) the black area is more than half.

**Answer: (A)**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-10.title: Count the digits
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-10.body:
The zeros come from $10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60$: exactly six zeros means the book ends at a page from 60 to 69. The eights so far: $8, 18, 28, 38, 48, 58$ — six of them; the seventh is $68$, and 69 would not add another. With seven 8s the last page must be at least 68, so it is 68 or 69 — among the choices, $68$.

**Answer: (B) 68**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-10.title: Check the choices
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-10.body:
58: only five zeros and six 8s. 68: zeros in 10–60 (six), eights in 8, 18, …, 68 (seven) ✓. 70 would have seven zeros; 78 and 98 even more.

**Answer: (B) 68**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-11.title: Read the strips
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-11.body:
The numbers are $15728$, $22\square04$ and $\square\square331$. Without the hidden digits they add up to $15728 + 22004 + 331 = 38063$. The hidden digits must make up $57263 - 38063 = 19200$. So the hidden digit in the second number (hundreds place) is 2, and the third number starts with 1 and 9. The hidden digits are 1, 2 and 9.

**Answer: (B) 1, 2 and 9**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-11.title: Column by column
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-11.body:
Units: $8 + 4 + 1 = 13$, carry 1. Tens: $2 + 0 + 3 + 1 = 6$ ✓. Hundreds: $7 + x + 3 = 12$, so $x = 2$, carry 1. Thousands: $5 + 2 + y + 1 = 17$, so $y = 9$, carry 1. Ten-thousands: $1 + 2 + z + 1 = 5$, so $z = 1$. Hidden digits: 1, 2, 9.

**Answer: (B) 1, 2 and 9**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-12.title: Start with the extremes
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-12.body:
Erika shakes 5 hands — with everybody. So Anna's only handshake is with Erika. Dora shakes 4 hands: everybody except herself and Anna, i.e. Bella, Claire, Erika, Frieda. Bella's two handshakes are with Erika and Dora. Claire's three: Erika, Dora and (not Anna, not Bella) Frieda. So Frieda shakes hands with Erika, Dora and Claire: 3 people.

**Answer: (C) 3**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-12.title: Parity check
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-12.body:
The total number of handshakes counted from each person is $1+2+3+4+5+f$, which must be even (each handshake is counted twice). So $f$ is odd: 1, 3 or 5. The detailed analysis above shows $f = 3$.

**Answer: (C) 3**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-13.title: Where is E?
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-13.body:
E lies on the perpendicular bisector of AC, which is the line BD. Going A → E → C anticlockwise means E is on the same side of AC as B. Since the triangle's height $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}AC$ is larger than $BO = \frac12 AC$ (O the centre), E lies on line DB beyond B.

So B lies between D and E on a straight line, and $\angle CBE = 180^\circ - \angle CBD = 180^\circ - 45^\circ = 135^\circ$.

**Answer: (C) 135°**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-13.title: Coordinates
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-13.body:
Take $A = (0,0)$, $B = (1,0)$, $C = (1,1)$, $D = (0,1)$. The point E with AEC equilateral and anticlockwise is $E = \left(\frac{1+\sqrt3}{2}, \frac{1-\sqrt3}{2}\right)$. Then $\vec{BC} = (0,1)$ and $\vec{BE} = \left(\frac{\sqrt3-1}{2}, -\frac{\sqrt3-1}{2}\right)$, which points at $-45^\circ$. The angle from $90^\circ$ to $-45^\circ$ is $135^\circ$.

**Answer: (C) 135°**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-14.title: Small numerators, big denominators
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-14.body:
To make the sum small, the numerators should be the smallest numbers 1 and 2 and the denominators the largest numbers 9 and 10. Two arrangements:

$\frac19 + \frac{2}{10} = \frac{10 + 18}{90} = \frac{28}{90} = \frac{14}{45}$, and $\frac{1}{10} + \frac29 = \frac{9 + 20}{90} = \frac{29}{90}$.

The smaller one is $\frac{14}{45}$ (put the bigger numerator over the bigger denominator).

**Answer: (C) $\frac{14}{45}$**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-15.title: Pick convenient numbers
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-15.body:
Let the flag be 3 high and 5 wide, area 15; each piece has area $\frac{15}{4}$. The dark strip on the left has full height 3, so its width is $\frac{15}{4} : 3 = \frac54$. The rest has width $5 - \frac54 = \frac{15}{4}$ and is split into three equal horizontal strips of height 1 each. So the white rectangle is $1 \times \frac{15}{4}$, ratio $1 : \frac{15}{4} = 4 : 15$.

**Answer: (E) 4 : 15**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-16.title: Start in the corners
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-16.body:
The figure has 12 cells, so it needs 4 L-pieces. Call the right block (2 columns, 4 rows) and the left block (2 columns, 2 rows) attached to its two middle rows.

- The two top cells of the right block can only be covered by pieces lying in its top $2\times2$ square; two different pieces would need 6 cells there, so **one** piece covers both top cells plus one cell below them. Likewise one piece covers both bottom cells plus one cell above.
- The two left-most cells (outer column of the left block) can only lie in the left $2\times 2$ square, so one piece covers both of them plus one of the two cells next to them.
- The last piece consists of the remaining cell of the left block and the two remaining cells in the middle rows of the right block. For this to be an L, those two cells must be the ones in the column next to the left block, so the top and bottom pieces must take the outer-column cells.

The only free choice is which cell of the left block's inner column the left piece takes (upper or lower): **2 ways**.

**Answer: (B) 2**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-17.title: Find the swimming fraction
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-17.body:
Cycling and running make $\frac34 + \frac15 = \frac{19}{20}$ of the distance, so swimming is $\frac{1}{20}$ of it. Since this is 2 km, the whole distance is $20\cdot 2 = 40$ km.

**Answer: (D) 40**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-17.title: Check
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-17.body:
For 40 km: cycling 30 km, running 8 km, swimming 2 km, total 40 ✓.

**Answer: (D) 40**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-18.title: Parts
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-18.body:
Ratio $1:7$ means 1 part syrup and 7 parts water, 8 parts juice. For 2 litres, one part is $\frac{2}{8} = \frac14$ litre, so $\frac14$ litre of syrup is needed. The bottle holds $\frac12$ litre, and $\frac14$ is half of it.

**Answer: (B) $\frac12$**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-18.title: Check
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-18.body:
Using half of the remaining $\frac12$ l gives $\frac14$ l syrup plus $\frac74$ l water $= 2$ l of juice ✓.

**Answer: (B) $\frac12$**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-19.title: Angles at the centres
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-19.body:
Take the middle circle and the left circle. Their centres are $R$ apart, and each intersection point is at distance $R$ from both centres, so it forms an equilateral triangle with them. Therefore, seen from either centre, the two intersection points are $2\cdot 60^\circ = 120^\circ$ apart.

- Each outer circle: its $120^\circ$ arc inside the middle circle is missing, so it contributes $240^\circ$, i.e. $\frac23\cdot 2\pi R$.
- The middle circle: $120^\circ$ lies inside the left circle and $120^\circ$ inside the right circle, so only $120^\circ$ remains on the boundary: $\frac13\cdot 2\pi R$.

Perimeter $= 2\cdot\frac43\pi R + \frac23\pi R = \frac{10\pi R}{3}$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac{10\pi R}{3}$**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-20.title: Set up an equation
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-20.body:
$3a + 4b = 10a + b$, so $3b = 7a$. As $a, b$ are digits and 3 and 7 share no factor, $a = 3$ and $b = 7$. Check: $3\cdot3 + 4\cdot 7 = 37$ ✓. So $a + b = 10$.

**Answer: (C) 10**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-21.title: Divisibility conditions
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-21.body:
Let the number be $10a + b$. Deleting a digit leaves $a$ or $b$, so we need $a \mid 10a + b$ and $b \mid 10a + b$ (in particular $b \neq 0$).

$a \mid 10a+b$ means $a \mid b$, so $b = ka$. Then $b \mid 10a + b$ means $ka \mid 10a$, i.e. $k \mid 10$, so $k \in \{1, 2, 5\}$ (since $b \le 9$).

- $k = 1$: $11, 22, \ldots, 99$ — 9 numbers.
- $k = 2$: $12, 24, 36, 48$ — 4 numbers.
- $k = 5$: $15$ — 1 number.

Total $9 + 4 + 1 = 14$.

**Answer: (C) 14**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-22.title: Two conditions on the number of boxes
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-22.body:
With $n$ boxes: the apples require $n \mid 60$. The pear counts are $n$ different positive numbers, so their sum is at least $1 + 2 + \dots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} \le 60$, which gives $n \le 10$. And $n = 10$ divides 60: 6 apples per box and pears $1, 2, \ldots, 9, 15$ (sum 60). So the maximum is 10.

**Answer: (D) 10**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-23.title: Close up the vertices with four faces
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-23.body:
At every vertex of an octahedron exactly 4 faces meet.

- The vertex at the top of the second triangle in the strip (where the top flap is attached) already has 4 triangles around it in the net. When folded, its two free edges join: so the top flap's free corner becomes the top vertex at the end of edge 2.
- Likewise the bottom vertex where the lower flap is attached has 4 triangles around it, so the lower flap's free corner joins the bottom vertex at the right end of edge 5.

So edge $x$ (from the bottom-right corner of the strip to the lower flap's corner) and edge 5 (along the bottom, ending at that same vertex) share a vertex. Continuing the same way, edge 3 is glued to edge 2, then edge 4 to edge 1, and finally edge 5 to edge $x$. So $x$ meets edge 5.

**Answer: (E) 5**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-24.title: Pythagoras from the centre
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-24.body:
By symmetry the square is centred on the centre O of the diameter. If the side is $s$, a top vertex is $\frac s2$ to the side of O and $s$ above it, and it lies on the circle: $\left(\frac s2\right)^2 + s^2 = 1$. So $\frac54 s^2 = 1$ and the area is $s^2 = \frac45$ cm².

**Answer: (A) $\frac45$ cm²**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-25.title: Speed is proportional to the radius
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-25.body:
Both points turn through the same angle, so the speed is proportional to the distance from the centre. If the inner point is $r$ from the centre: $r + 3 = 2.5r$, so $r = 2$ and the outer point is $5$ cm from the centre.

**Answer: (E) 5 cm**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-25.title: Test the choices
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-25.body:
Outer 5 cm, inner 2 cm: ratio $5 : 2 = 2.5$ ✓. Outer 6: inner 3, ratio 2. Outer 10: inner 7, ratio $\approx 1.43$. Only 5 cm works.

**Answer: (E) 5 cm**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-26.title: Structure of the triples
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-26.body:
After 1–9 (three triples), the two-digit numbers come in groups of three numbers $m, m+1, m+2$ with $m = 10, 13, 16, \ldots$ (i.e. $m \equiv 1 \pmod 3$). Each group gives two triples: (both digits of $m$, first digit of $m+1$) and (second digit of $m+1$, both digits of $m+2$).

- (222): $m = 22$, then $23$ starts with 2 ✓.
- (888): $m = 88$, then $89$ ✓.
- (464): $m = 46$, then $47$ ✓.
- (646): $m = 64$ ($64 - 10 = 54$ is a multiple of 3), then $65$ starts with 6 ✓.
- (444): first type needs $m = 44$, but $44 \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ ✗; second type needs $m + 2 = 44$, $m = 42 \equiv 0$ ✗.

So (444) never appears.

**Answer: (B) (444)**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-27.title: Classify planes through three vertices
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-27.body:
Any three vertices of a cube either lie on a face, on a diagonal rectangle (through two opposite edges), or form an equilateral triangle of face diagonals. Faces and diagonal rectangles contain 4 vertices each, so they don't count. The remaining planes are the ones through the three neighbours of a vertex (cutting off that corner). Each vertex gives one such plane, and these planes contain exactly 3 vertices. So there are $8$ of them.

**Answer: (D) 8**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-28.title: Colour the points in two colours
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-28.body:
Colour the points of the outer octagon alternately black and white, starting with A black, and colour each inner point with the opposite colour of the outer point it is joined to. Then every line joins two points of different colours (the inner octagon also alternates, because 8 is even). So each move changes the colour, and after an odd number of moves — such as 2019 — the ant is on a white point.

Number the outer points $0$ (A) to $7$ clockwise. T and R are outer points 2 and 4, so they are black. Q is joined to outer point 4 (black), so Q is white; P and S are joined to outer points 5 and 3 (white), so they are black. Hence after 2019 moves the ant cannot be at P, R, S or T. It can be at Q: walk $A 	o 1 	o 2 	o 3 	o 4 	o Q$ (5 moves) and then go back and forth along one line 1007 times ($5 + 2014 = 2019$). So the answer is: only at Q.

**Answer: (C) only at Q**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-29.title: Bound and check
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-29.body:
$c = 4a + 3 \le 999$ gives $a \le 249$, so $a$ starts (and ends) with 1 or 2.

- If $a = \overline{2x2}$: $b = 2a + 1$ ends in 5, so it must start with 5, but then $c = 2b + 1 > 1000$. Impossible.
- If $a = \overline{1x1}$: $b = 2a + 1 = 203 + 20x$ ends in 3, so it must start with 3: $x \ge 5$, giving $b \in \{303, 323, 343, 363, 383\}$. Then $c = 2b + 1 \in \{607, 647, 687, 727, 767\}$ ends in 7 and must start with 7: $c = 727$ or $767$.

So $a = 181$ ($b = 363$, $c = 727$) or $a = 191$ ($b = 383$, $c = 767$): **2** values.

**Answer: (C) 2**

kangaroo-at-2019-junior-30.title: Prime factorisation
kangaroo-at-2019-junior-30.body:
The product is $10^9\cdot 9! = 2^9 5^9 \cdot 2^7 3^4 5\cdot 7 = 2^{16}\, 3^4\, 5^{10}\, 7$.

The factor 7 appears only in 70, so 70 must be removed; that leaves $2^{15} 3^4 5^9$, which is not a square. So one removal is not enough. Removing 70 and 10 leaves $2^{14} 3^4 5^8$, a square. The minimum is **2**.

**Answer: (B) 2**
